RRSP over-contribution: what the CAD 2,000 cushion covers, how the 1% month-end tax adds up, and why the dates of your deposits matter

Follow the Income Tax Act’s cumulative excess amount month by month: where the CAD 2,000 cushion fits, why a withdrawal before the month-end avoids that month’s tax, how new room in January absorbs an excess, what CRA assumes when you cannot show the months, and how median contributions compare with the cushion.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Without a withdrawal, your contributions first go more than $2,000 over your room in August 2026. The tax is 1% of the cumulative excess at the end of each month. With your inputs it runs for 2 months: $30.00 for 2026, against $200.00 with no withdrawal. Withdrawing $5,000 before the end of August 2026 would cost $0.00. If CRA has no records of the months, its default placement gives $450.00. Form T1-OVP and payment for 2026 are due by 31 March 2027.

The central idea

You can have up to CAD 2,000 of contributions above your RRSP deduction limit without tax, if you turned 18 before the year. Above that, the cumulative excess is taxed at 1% at the end of every month it remains. Because the test is the month-end, withdrawing the excess before the end of the month it appears avoids the tax entirely, unlike a TFSA. New room each January absorbs an excess, but payroll contributions can create it again. Keep statements with transaction dates: without them, CRA may place deposits in January or March and withdrawals in December, which can multiply the tax. In 2023 the median RRSP contribution was CAD 4,000.

01

How people end up over their RRSP limit

Most registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) over-contributions are not deliberate. A payroll plan keeps deducting every month after a bonus has gone in as a lump sum; the deduction limit on last year’s notice of assessment was read before a pension adjustment was counted; or contributions made in the first 60 days of the year were meant for last year’s return but last year’s room was already full. The Income Tax Act allows a small margin for this, then charges 1% a month on the rest.

The calculator follows that rule month by month for 2026 and 2027, with a monthly contribution, one lump sum, one withdrawal and the new room that arrives in January 2027. It answers four questions: when does the tax start, how much does the timing of a withdrawal change it, does new room fix the problem, and what happens if you cannot prove the months.

02

The cumulative excess, in the Act’s terms

Section 204.2(1.1) of the Income Tax Act defines the cumulative excess amount at any time in a year as your undeducted RRSP premiums minus A + B + R + C + D + E, if positive. For most people, the pieces reduce to three:

ElementMeaningIn the calculator
Undeducted premiumsContributions not yet deducted from earlier years, plus contributions paid this year so far, minus withdrawals that are included in incomeCarried-in amount, monthly and one-time contributions, withdrawal
A + B (+ R)Unused room at the end of last year, plus this year’s new room and any pension adjustment reversal: the deduction limit on your notice of assessmentRRSP deduction limit for 2026; new room for 2027
CCAD 2,000 if you turned 18 in an earlier year; otherwise nil“Turned 18 before 2026”

D (a group plan amount) and E (a transitional amount for people who were 18 before 1995) apply in narrower cases and are taken as nil here.

Section 204.1(2.1) then imposes a tax for each month equal to 1% of the cumulative excess at the end of the month. That last phrase is the important difference from a TFSA, where the tax is 1% of the highest excess at any time in the month: see the TFSA over-contribution guide. CRA’s excess contributions page says the same in plain terms: you may not owe the tax on amounts withdrawn before the end of the month in which the excess contribution was made.

  • The cushion is a fixed dollar amount. CAD 2,000 is written into the Act and is not indexed, while the RRSP dollar limit rises each year: CAD 33,810 for 2026 and CAD 35,390 for 2027, according to CRA’s limits table.
  • The cushion is not extra room. Contributions inside it are not deductible until new room arrives; they are simply not taxed while they wait.
  • The tax is not prorated or compounded. Each month-end’s excess is charged 1%, and the months are added up.

03

Four worked cases

All four use the calculator’s default: a CAD 15,000 deduction limit for 2026 and nothing carried in; CAD 1,000 a month by payroll through 2026; a CAD 10,000 lump sum in March; CAD 9,000 of new room for 2027; and CAD 500 a month in 2027. With the cushion, contributions can reach CAD 17,000 in 2026 before tax applies. They reach CAD 18,000 by the end of August.

  1. Nothing withdrawn. The month-end excess is CAD 1,000 in August, then CAD 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 and 5,000 to December: 1% of the total CAD 15,000 is CAD 150 for 2026. On 1 January 2027 the new room of CAD 9,000 absorbs the overage, but CAD 500 a month rebuilds it, and the cumulative excess returns in September 2027: CAD 500 to CAD 2,000 for four months, another CAD 50. Total CAD 200.
  2. CAD 5,000 withdrawn in October (the default). August and September are taxed at CAD 10 and CAD 20: CAD 30. After the withdrawal, contributions stay within room plus cushion through 2027.
  3. CAD 5,000 withdrawn in August, before that month-end. No month-end ever shows an excess: nil. Under the TFSA rule, the same timing would still cost a month.
  4. Case 2 when CRA has no dates. If the October withdrawal is placed in December and the payroll contributions from March on are placed in March, the excess is CAD 5,000 at every month-end from March to November: 9 × CAD 50 = CAD 450, fifteen times the CAD 30 from the real dates.

The second chart follows your inputs month by month. The third repeats them with the withdrawal moved to every possible month. The fourth compares your months with CRA’s default placement.

04

Withdrawing the excess: timing and the income tax side

Because only month-ends count, the cheapest moment to withdraw is before the end of the month in which the excess first appears. Every later month-end adds 1% of what is still over. Two practical points make the withdrawal less simple than it sounds:

  • The withdrawal is income. An RRSP withdrawal is included in income, even when it returns contributions that were never deducted. CRA’s RRSP guide (T4040) explains that you may be able to deduct an equal amount on line 23200, calculated on Form T746, if you withdraw the unused contributions in the year they were made, the following year, or the year a notice of assessment or reassessment for the contribution year is issued or the year after. Outside those windows the same dollars can be taxed on the way out without ever having been deducted.
  • Tax is withheld unless you ask first. To have the issuer pay out unused contributions without withholding, Form T3012A has to be approved by CRA before the withdrawal; that takes time, so the month-end tax may keep running while you wait. The withholding guide shows how withheld tax is settled on the return.

Waiting for new room is the alternative. In January each year the new room (18% of last year’s earned income up to the dollar limit, less any pension adjustment) absorbs an excess first. That only ends the tax if contributions in the new year do not rebuild it, which case 1 shows payroll deductions can do.

05

Why the dates of each deposit matter

RRSP receipts and T4RSP slips do not show the month of a contribution or a withdrawal, and CRA says it will not accept them as proof of those months. Its T1-OVP instructions say that without documents it may place contributions from the first 60 days of the year in January, the rest of the year’s contributions in March, and withdrawals in December.

Every one of those moves pushes deposits earlier or withdrawals later, so the default placement can only increase the tax. The fourth chart shows the gap for your inputs. A monthly statement or transaction history from the issuer showing each date is the evidence to keep with Form T1-OVP.

06

How the CAD 2,000 compares with ordinary contributions

Statistics Canada’s Table 11-10-0044-01 (released 1 April 2025, latest year 2023) counts tax filers with RRSP contributions. The cushion has not moved while typical contributions have grown.

Tax yearTax filersRRSP contributorsMedian contributionCushion as % of median
200021,611,8306,291,170CAD 2,70074%
201024,494,9405,956,010CAD 2,79072%
201927,171,9905,912,000CAD 3,26061%
202329,965,1006,350,070CAD 4,00050%

In 2023 about 21% of tax filers contributed, and total contributions were about CAD 55.7 billion. The median is the middle contributor, so half contributed more than CAD 4,000 in the year; for many of them a single extra payroll month or a misread room figure is more than the cushion. Statistics Canada and CRA do not publish counts of people with an excess or the Part X.1 tax collected in these tables, so the first chart is context, not a count of people taxed.

07

If you are already over

  1. Stop or reduce automatic contributions until new room arrives, or the excess keeps growing.
  2. Withdraw the amount over room plus CAD 2,000, ideally before a month-end, after weighing the withholding and the line 23200 deduction above.
  3. File Form T1-OVP and pay within 90 days after the end of the year with the excess: by 31 March 2027 for 2026. The guide lists a late-filing penalty of 5% of the balance owing plus 1% a month for up to 12 months, and interest.
  4. Ask for a waiver if it was a reasonable error. Section 204.1(4) lets the Minister waive the tax if the excess arose from reasonable error and reasonable steps are being taken to eliminate it. The request is made on Form RC2503; withdraw or otherwise fix the excess first.

08

What the calculator leaves out

  • Pension adjustments and reversals. Enter your deduction limit and new room after them; the calculator does not compute them.
  • Group plans and pre-1995 transitional amounts (elements D and E) are taken as nil.
  • Several withdrawals, transfers and special withdrawals. Home Buyers’ Plan and Lifelong Learning Plan withdrawals may not remove the excess for this tax, CRA notes, and transfers from pensions or retiring allowances have their own rules.
  • Growth, penalties and interest. Amounts are contributions, not market values, and late-filing penalties and interest are not included.
  • Age 18. The cushion applies only if you turned 18 in an earlier year; someone who turns 18 during 2026 has no cushion until 2027, which the single yes/no input does not separate.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. The first chart shows Statistics Canada Table 11-10-0044-01 (released 1 April 2025; latest reference year 2023). The other three apply sections 204.1 and 204.2 of the Income Tax Act (current to 30 September 2026) and CRA’s RRSP pages, reviewed 27 October 2026, to hypothetical editable inputs for 2026 and 2027. Group plan amounts, pension adjustment reversals, transitional amounts, investment growth, penalties and interest are not included. These are planning estimates, not CRA’s assessment.   2. Justice Laws · Income Tax Act, section 204.2 (cumulative excess amount) ↗

    Act current to 30 September 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026.
